title: Tanbura (six-string lyre)
summary: The tanbura is a six-string lyre of the Red Sea coast and Nubia. A wide, shallow bowl is covered with hide and studded at the rim; two short, thick arms are set with cowrie shells and carry a square crossbar lashed with rope. It is plucked and strummed to carry dance songs.
howToPlay: Six strings run from the rope-lashed crossbar to the bridge, the lowest on the left. Each lane marks a place to pluck one string.
Beads slide down the strings. Pluck the lane as the bead lands.
The songs repeat a short figure over and over, as in dance music.
Start slowly with the first figure, then speed up as it settles.
rules: The six strings are tuned to a scale with a lowered seventh.
Every figure is played through twice.
A stroke on the beat is perfect, a near one is good, and extra strokes cost points.
Figures count four beats to the bar, with a lift on the last.
heritageNote: In the ports and villages of the Red Sea coast the tanbura accompanies songs for gatherings and work. Its wide bowl gives a low, rounded note, and the cowrie shells on the arms are an old mark of the coast.
